name: Hijack a vehicle
summary: A unit takes an enemy vehicle away from its crew and turns it to its own side, whole and working. Usually the hijacker reaches the vehicle and climbs in: the driver is thrown out or killed, at once or after a short struggle that holds the target still, and the hijacker drives it until it is destroyed, often stepping out of the wreck. A ranged twist kills the crew with one special shot or blast instead and leaves the hull empty and neutral for whoever climbs in first, of either side. Only crewed vehicles can be taken: drones and robots are immune, aircraft are out of reach in the strategy games, and some protect a loaded transport. Hijackers are mostly fragile soldiers who must get close unseen. Borrowing a unit's weapon is mind-control; taking a building is capture-structure.
counterplay: Shoot the hijacker before it arrives: most are unarmed or fragile soldiers, so anti-infantry escorts and machine guns stop them (Generals Pathfinders; Halo Wars 2 players keep anti-infantry near their armour to stop a takeover).
Field vehicles with no crew: drones and robots cannot be hijacked or emptied (the Generals Sentry Drone), and the Generals Hijacker cannot reach aircraft at all.
Keep moving: a vehicle that never slows down is very hard to board in Halo, and the driver or a gunner can run the boarder over or shoot it.
Bring detection: hijackers often hide until the last moment, so a detector or a stealth-spotting weapon (the Overlord's gattling add-on in Generals) exposes them.

Keep riders aboard: since a Zero Hour patch the Hijacker cannot take a transport with anyone inside, such as a loaded Battle Bus, though Jarmen Kell's crew snipe still empties it and pushes the riders out.

Take it back or deny it: an ejected driver can board again, teammates can kill the hijacker inside, your own infantry can reclaim an emptied hull first, or you can destroy your own vehicle before the thief drives off (a sticky grenade after being thrown out, in Halo).
Interrupt the takeover: where it takes time (Halo Wars), killing the hijacker during the struggle cancels it.

other_examples.note: An unarmed soldier, hidden while it stands still (Kassad's version stays hidden on the move), that takes most enemy vehicles the instant it reaches them and keeps their veterancy; it can survive the destruction of some American vehicles. It cannot take aircraft, uncrewed drones such as the Sentry Drone, or, since a Zero Hour patch, a transport with anyone inside, and Pathfinders and stealth-spotting gattling guns pick it off. Players hide it beside a busy route or let a visible unit lure a vehicle so the hijacker can slip in.

other_examples.unit: Neutron Shells and Neutron Mines (China, Zero Hour)
other_examples.note: The area version of the crew kill. Nuke Cannon shells and mines bought for a base's buildings kill every soldier in the blast and the crew and passengers of every vehicle, whatever its armour, while barely scratching the hulls; the empty vehicles turn neutral until any soldier climbs in. Workers and dozers can find and remove the mines.

A commando, one at a time, who can steal any vehicle, the heaviest walkers and construction vehicles included. Once inside he cannot be removed until the vehicle is destroyed; then he steps out and can steal another.

sources.title: Mutant hijacker, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its quote box copies the Tiberian Sun manual entry.

other_examples.note: Spartan heroes take over enemy vehicles, more slowly than in the shooters. A vehicle driven by a Spartan gets better stats and earns veterancy faster, and the Spartan walks out unharmed when it is destroyed. In Halo Wars 2 the Spartan leaps on with a slam that stuns nearby enemies, the target cannot move until the takeover ends, and killing the Spartan meanwhile cancels it, so opponents keep anti-infantry units near their best vehicles.

sources.title: Red Team, Halopedia
sources.note: Gameplay sections on both Halo Wars games.

sources.title: Jerome-092/Gameplay, Halopedia
sources.note: His Hijack upgrade, and the counter advice to keep anti-infantry units near vehicles.

shooter_analogues.note: Holding the action button beside an enemy vehicle kicks the driver out and puts the boarder in the seat; the danger is being run over or shot by a gunner on the way in. Some vehicles only lose their driver, and on tanks the boarder instead smashes the hatch or drops a grenade inside. An EMP shot that stalls the engine makes boarding easy. The victim avoids it by never slowing down, can board again after being thrown out, or blows up the vehicle to deny it.

In these top-down shooters the player boards an enemy tank from either side, just behind its fins, and risks being crushed on the approach; after the takeover the Elite driver is punched out. Wearing the tank down first forces the Elites out, an easier route to the seat.

sources.title: Boarding (gameplay mechanic), Halopedia
sources.note: The part about the two top-down Spartan games.

player_translation.summary: A fragile infiltrator whose prize is the enemy's vehicle. Getting there is the game: sneak or bait your way close, win a short struggle, throw the driver out and play the vehicle until it dies. The ranged variant empties a vehicle with one shot and starts a race to climb in.
as_user: You buy a light infantry unit with little firepower; your real weapon is the enemy's vehicle.

Get beside a crewed enemy vehicle and hold the key: after a short struggle (quicker from behind, or while the vehicle is stalled) the driver is thrown out and you take the seat with its current health, ammo and weapons.

You then play the vehicle until it is destroyed, when you step out of the wreck on foot with a moment of protection, ready for the next one. A stolen vehicle never counts as yours for buying or upgrades.
Drones, robots and aircraft refuse you, and so does a transport with riders aboard; an icon on them says so before you commit.
Crew-snipe variant: one special shot at a crewed vehicle in range throws its driver out stunned and leaves the hull neutral, and the first player of either side to climb in takes it.
as_target: An alarm and an arrow show who is climbing on, and the struggle gives you a moment to react: speed up, swerve, ram, or let a teammate shoot the boarder off.
Hold the shake-off key to make the struggle last longer.
If the takeover completes you are thrown out alive as a weak crew unit beside your old vehicle, briefly stunned; you can board again if the thief dies or gets out, or help your team destroy it.
Against the crew-snipe your hull stands empty: race your team to it before the sniper's teammates arrive.
teammates: The hijacker's team sets the boarding up: an EMP or a stun stalls the vehicle, bait draws its fire, and escorts walk the hijacker in.
The victim's team keeps anti-infantry escorts and detectors near its armour, and brings crewless drones that cannot be taken.
A crew-snipe turns a vehicle into loot: whichever team's soldiers reach the empty hull first win it, so the sniper's teammates should be ready to move.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse; left mouse fires the hijacker's small arms, if it has any.
Hold E (signature) beside a crewed enemy vehicle to board; releasing E cancels. It is kept apart from the universal enter key so nobody boards an enemy by accident. One counted key.
Crew-snipe variant: Q fires the special round; anyone then claims the empty hull with the universal enter key.
Victim: hold F, the universal shake-off key, during the struggle.
feedback: A struggle ring in the hijacker's colour around the vehicle, an alarm for the driver and a minimap ping for the driver's team.
On takeover the vehicle's outline, nameplate and minimap marker switch to the hijacker's team colour with a flash, and the kill feed shows a hijack entry.
Emptied hulls are drawn grey with a claim icon visible to both teams.
Vehicles that cannot be taken show a small lock icon to an enemy hijacker close by.
changes_from_rts: In Generals a hijack is instant on contact; against a player that is a sudden loss with nothing to do about it, so the player version adds a short visible struggle, as Halo Wars does, which the driver can fight.
An RTS player just loses a unit; here the victim bought that vehicle, so they are thrown out alive as a weak crew unit and can win it back, rather than dying with no say.
Jarmen Kell's snipe leaves the hull to whichever soldiers reach it; in a shooter the race to the empty vehicle becomes a small objective both teams can see.
The thief keeps the vehicle until it is destroyed, as in Generals and Tiberian Sun, but cannot repair, sell or upgrade it, so a theft swings a fight without becoming a money exploit.
Immunities (crewless machines, aircraft, loaded transports) stay, but they must show on the target.

team_play.notes: Boarding works best when a teammate stalls or baits the vehicle first, and a crew-snipe hands an empty vehicle to whichever team claims it, so the spoils are shared. The other team answers by escorting armour with anti-infantry and detectors and by fielding crewless machines.

notes: Moving a live vehicle between teams mid-match, with its health, ammo, cooldowns and seats, is new plumbing.
Both players change state: the victim becomes a crew unit on foot, and the hijacker's own unit is set aside and returns when the vehicle dies.
The struggle needs animations, interruption by damage and rules for edge cases: riders inside, a second boarder, the vehicle dying mid-struggle, a teammate of the thief already aboard.
The crew-snipe variant needs a neutral-hull state that either team can claim.
Scoring and economy: who gets credit for kills made with a stolen vehicle, and whether the victim gets anything back.
A cheap unit taking the enemy's most expensive vehicle is a huge swing; the struggle time, the immunities and the hijacker's fragility are the levers.
A crew-snipe from long range with no warning can empty a heavy tank in one shot; keep it on a long cooldown, on a high tier and visible in flight.
Chain theft (step out of one wreck, steal the next) can snowball; a short cooldown after stepping out keeps it fair.
If crewless machines are the only answer, they become mandatory picks once hijackers are common.
Everyone must see at once that a vehicle changed sides, or teammates will be shot by what looks like a friendly tank.
A neutral hull needs a look of its own, distinct from both teams and from wrecks.
The struggle must be readable from above even in a crowded fight.

variants.name: Board and take
variants.summary: Reach a crewed enemy vehicle and take it after a short struggle; the driver is thrown out, and you drive it until it is destroyed, then step out of the wreck. The default.
variants.seen_in: Generals Hijacker, Tiberian Sun Mutant Hijacker, Halo boarding

variants.name: Instant steal
variants.summary: No struggle: touching the vehicle takes it at once, so the hijacker must stay hidden until the last moment and is helpless once seen.

variants.name: Pin, then take
variants.summary: The hijacker leaps on with a slam that stuns enemies nearby; the vehicle cannot move while the takeover runs, and killing the hijacker cancels it.

variants.name: Ace driver
variants.summary: A vehicle you drive gets better stats and keeps or gains veterancy, and you step out unharmed when it is destroyed.
variants.seen_in: Halo Wars Spartans, Tiberian Sun Mutant Hijacker, Generals Hijacker (keeps the vehicle's rank)

variants.name: Crew snipe
variants.summary: One special shot from range kills a crewed vehicle's driver whatever its armour; the hull stops, turns neutral and goes to whoever climbs in first, of either side, and riders of a transport are pushed out.

variants.name: Crew-kill blast
variants.summary: A shell or a mine kills the crews of every vehicle in its blast and the soldiers there, leaving a cluster of neutral hulls for anyone's infantry to claim.
variants.seen_in: Generals Zero Hour Nuke Cannon neutron shells and neutron mines

adds_strengths.why: Turns an enemy vehicle, armour and guns included, into its own ride, so the enemy loses what it paid for and the hijacker gains it.

adds_weaknesses.why: Must get right next to the vehicle, or in clear line for the shot, while fragile and lightly armed, and crewless machines and aircraft are immune.

counters.why: Any vehicle with someone inside can be taken or emptied, whatever its armour or health.
Armour gives no protection, so the heaviest tanks are the best prizes.

countered_by.why: Drones and robots have no crew to remove, so they are immune and free to hunt the hijacker.
Anti-infantry escorts gun the fragile hijacker down before it reaches a vehicle or during the takeover.
Aircraft cannot be hijacked and kill a hijacker on foot without risk.
Hijackers rely on staying hidden until the last moment, and a detector exposes them.

open_questions: When a player's vehicle is hijacked, is the driver thrown out alive as a weak crew unit (the proposal here), killed, or paid back part of the price?
Can a hijacker take every vehicle class, or are walkers and huge vehicles exempt? Tiberian Sun lets its hijacker take even the heaviest walkers.
Does a stolen vehicle keep its owner's upgrades and loadout, and who is credited with its kills?
Crew snipe: should the empty hull be open to anyone, as in Generals, or reserved for the sniper's team for a moment?
Should a transport with riders aboard be immune to boarding, as in Zero Hour since patch 1.03?

The crew snipe is written as a variant here, following the registry note that folds it into this pattern, because the target ends up the same (a working vehicle changes hands and crewless machines are immune); if the merge pass treats the neutral-hull race as its own interaction, the variant could move out as a separate id.

shooter_fit.reason: Halo made boarding a staple of shooters, its top-down Spartan Assault included, and stealing a tank is a memorable swing. Against players it needs a visible struggle, a way to fight back and a driver who survives the ejection, or it feels like losing a purchase for nothing.
